title: Universal Subdivision Engine & Path Geometry Architecture

This archive preserves the project’s original rationale, equations, performance reports and illustrative code. Historical paths, API names, claims and sketches can differ from the current engine. For copy-ready programs use the guides and demos; for current callable signatures use the source-derived API. Performance figures here describe reported experiments, not guaranteed frame rates.

blocks.text: Original document: [docs/SUBDIVISION_AND_PATH_GEOMETRY_ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/abhilasbiswas/Retiam/blob/main/docs/SUBDIVISION_AND_PATH_GEOMETRY_ARCHITECTURE.md). See [current limitations](/limitations) for concrete compatibility notes.

This document provides a comprehensive, mathematically rigorous, and structural technical manual for the **Universal Subdivision Engine (`SubdivisionEngine`)** and **Path Geometry Utilities (`PathGeometryUtils`)** within the Retiam WebGPU animation engine.

In computer graphics, 2D/3D computer-aided geometric design (CAGD), and real-time GPU animation, vector paths and polygons are fundamentally defined by sparse sets of discrete control vertices $\mathcal{P} = \{\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{p}_1, \dots, \mathbf{p}_{N-1}\}$. While sparse representations are optimal for storage, authoring, and linear affine transforms ($\mathbf{M}\mathbf{p}$), they fail in three critical operational scenarios:

items: **Non-Linear Spatial Deformations & Homotopies**: Non-affine spatial transforms (e.g., sine wave warps, vortices, spherical projections, gravitational bends) evaluate coordinates point-wise: $\mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p})$. If an entity has only 2 vertices (such as a straight line), the function transforms only its endpoints, leaving the segment as a rigid straight stick that shears or rotates rather than bending into a curve.

**Non-Uniform Arc-Length Velocity**: Traversal along raw polylines with varying segment lengths causes severe acceleration spikes. Parametric stepping along raw vertices produces non-physical motion unless paths are re-parameterized by cumulative arc length:

**Analytical Curve Splitting & Tessellation**: Higher-order polynomial curves (Quadratic and Cubic Bézier curves) require exact algebraic subdivision (via de Casteljau's algorithm) to enable clipping, adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) flattening, and bounding box hierarchy computation without numerical drift.

blocks.text: To solve these problems systematically across all Retiam primitives (`Poly`, `Line`, `Line3D`, `NumberPlane`, `Path`, `PixelGrid`, `MeshSprite`), Retiam provides **`SubdivisionEngine`** (`src/engine/utils/SubdivisionEngine.ts`) and **`PathGeometryUtils`** (`src/engine/utils/PathGeometryUtils.ts`).
The subdivision architecture operates as a foundational mathematical utility layer beneath Retiam's scene graph and GPU rendering pipelines:

blocks.text: In adaptive modes, long segments receive proportionally more cuts, whereas short segments receive fewer cuts. This ensures **uniform spatial vertex density** without wasteful over-sampling on short edges.
`SubdivisionEngine` and `PathGeometryUtils` handle 7 distinct algorithmic use cases, each serving specific geometric, kinematic, and rendering requirements.

Given an open sequence of 3D points $\mathbf{P} = (\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{p}_1, \dots, \mathbf{p}_{M-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^3$, each segment $i \in [0, M-2]$ with direction vector $\mathbf{d}_i = \mathbf{p}_{i+1} - \mathbf{p}_i$ and length $L_i = \|\mathbf{d}_i\|$ is interpolated linearly:
The final vertex $\mathbf{p}_{M-1}$ is appended at the terminal boundary.

items: Supports 3D spatial points ($\text{Vec3}$).
Seamlessly transitions between fixed subdivision counts and metric-adaptive `maxSegmentLength`.
Produces $1 + \sum_{i=0}^{M-2} S_i$ total vertices.

blocks.text: For a closed $N$-gon defined by perimeter vertices $\mathbf{P} = (\mathbf{p}_0, \mathbf{p}_1, \dots, \mathbf{p}_{N-1}) \in \mathbb{R}^2$, subdivision must cycle back from the final vertex to the origin:

Standard polygons (e.g., star, pentagon, hexagon) only contain vertices at their sharp corners. Without perimeter subdivision, applying spatial deformations or vertex kinematics leaves the edges completely rigid and straight. `subdivideClosedPolygon2D` generates dense perimeter samples along all edges including the closing seam ($P_{N-1} \to P_0$), enabling smooth ripple, wave, or scallop morphing.
Case 3: De Casteljau Analytical Bézier Splitting (splitQuadraticBezier & splitCubicBezier)

Given a cubic Bézier curve defined by control points $\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \mathbf{P}_3 \in \mathbb{R}^2$ and a split parameter $t \in (0, 1)$, de Casteljau's algorithm recursively computes convex combinations:

blocks.tex:
\begin{aligned}
\text{Level 1:} \quad \mathbf{Q}_0 &= (1-t)\mathbf{P}_0 + t\mathbf{P}_1 \\
\mathbf{Q}_1 &= (1-t)\mathbf{P}_1 + t\mathbf{P}_2 \\
\mathbf{Q}_2 &= (1-t)\mathbf{P}_2 + t\mathbf{P}_3 \\[6pt]
\text{Level 2:} \quad \mathbf{R}_0 &= (1-t)\mathbf{Q}_0 + t\mathbf{Q}_1 \\
\mathbf{R}_1 &= (1-t)\mathbf{Q}_1 + t\mathbf{Q}_2 \\[6pt]
\text{Level 3 (Split Apex):} \quad \mathbf{S} &= (1-t)\mathbf{R}_0 + t\mathbf{R}_1
\end{aligned}

blocks.text: The curve is split into two independent, mathematically exact cubic Bézier curves:

items: **Exact Algebraic Representation**: Zero chord error, polynomial degree elevation, or numerical re-fitting.
**$C^1$ Continuity**: The tangent vectors of both curves at the split point $\mathbf{S}$ are strictly collinear:

blocks.text: By repeatedly applying de Casteljau splitting at midpoint $t = 0.5$ to recursion depth $d$, a single cubic Bézier curve is subdivided into $2^d$ smaller cubic sub-segments:
Let $\text{CH}(\mathbf{P}_0, \mathbf{P}_1, \mathbf{P}_2, \mathbf{P}_3)$ denote the convex hull of the Bézier control polygon. Under midpoint subdivision:

The control polygons shrinkwrap onto the true continuous curve at a quadratic rate $\mathcal{O}(4^{-d})$. At depth $d = 4$ (16 segments), the piecewise control polygon is virtually indistinguishable from the analytical curve. This algorithm forms the foundation of GPU font rendering, curve ray-tracing, and intersection testing.
Case 5: Uniform Arc-Length Resampling vs. Linear Subdivision (resampleByArcLength)

items: **Linear Subdivision (`subdividePolyline`)**: Divides each segment proportionally. If segment A is 20 units long and segment B is 2 units long, with `subdivisions: 5`, points on A are 4 units apart, while points on B are 0.4 units apart. The distribution depends entirely on waypoint placement.
**Arc-Length Resampling (`resampleByArcLength`)**: Parameterizes the path by cumulative arc length:

blocks.text: It distributes exactly $K$ sample points at strictly equal Euclidean intervals:
Each sample $\tilde{s}_j$ is located via binary/linear search across the cumulative length table and interpolated between adjacent waypoints.
When an animated entity or camera moves along a path at a fixed frame rate:

items: On a **linearly subdivided path**, velocity spikes across long segments and drops across short segments ($\Delta s / \Delta t \ne \text{const}$).
On an **arc-length resampled path**, physical velocity is strictly constant:

blocks.text: In real-time graphics engines, instantiating thousands of JavaScript `Vec3` objects per frame induces garbage collection (GC) pressure and CPU stalls. `subdividePackedVertices3D` operates directly on flat `Float32Array` memory buffers with a 4-float stride matching WebGPU's `vec4<f32>` alignment requirements:

blocks.tex: \text{Memory Layout: } [x_0, y_0, z_0, \text{pad}_0, \; x_1, y_1, z_1, \text{pad}_1, \; \dots, \; x_{N-1}, y_{N-1}, z_{N-1}, \text{pad}_{N-1}]

items: **Pass 1 (Length & Step Evaluation)**: Evaluates segment lengths directly from the raw float buffer indices (`in1 = i * 4`, `in2 = (i + 1) * 4`), computing segment steps via `resolveSegmentSteps`.
**Pass 2 (Single Allocation)**: Allocates a single destination `Float32Array(totalVertices * 4)`.
**Pass 3 (Vectorized Interpolation)**: Fills output floats sequentially without allocating any temporary objects.
**GPU Upload**: The resulting buffer can be written directly to a WebGPU storage or vertex buffer:
